newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil coffee crop benefits from recent rains.
newsitem.headline: Brazil coffee crop benefits from recent rains.

text.p: Rains over the past two months in Brazil's coffee regions have been beneficial for bean formation but cooperative officials see no reason to revise up 1997/98 crop forecasts of a maximum 20 million 60-kg bags.

"The rains have been excellent and have greatly helped the beans. But I think the crop will be no bigger than 19 million to 20 million bags," said Antonio Araujo da Silva, commercial director at the Varginha cooperative in south Minas Gerais.

"Before I was looking at an average of 19 million bags...and for the time being I don't see any reason to change," said Jose Braz Matiello, agronomist at the Procafe division of the Agriculture Ministry.
Yesterday the Brazilian Coffee Exporters' Association said it expected the coming harvest to be 23.2 million bags after conducting a survey amongst its members.
This figure was seen as fair by other traders in Brazil, including Jair Coser, president of leading exporter Unicafe.
"I think that at the most the crop will reach 22 million to 23 million. Anything well above that is exaggerated in the same way as 17 million or 18 million bags is exaggerated," he said.
One of the features of the 1997/98 harvest has been the scattered flowerings, which agronomists believe may have been caused by the extended period of low temperatures last winter.
But production in only one area, that of Espirito Santo, has been severely disrupted by the irregular blossoming, said an independent agronomist, recently returned from a field trip.
Coffee trees in the state look well, with healthy green leaves but there have been fewer flowerings than usual, said Unicafe's Coser who has a plantation in Espirito Santo.
"The prettier the tree, the greater the indication that it is not bearing a great deal," Matiello said.
The state of Espirito Santo Coser reckons will produce around four million bags in 1997/98, three million of which will be conillon coffee.
This is slightly higher than a forecast of 3.59 million bags made by the state agricultural secretariat in December, with the increase due to the benefits of the rains, Coser said.
However it is still well below the 4.97 million bags which the secretariat estimates was produced in 1996/97.
In addition to scattered flowerings, one other feature this year is almost constant blossoming in some regions which is carrying on even through this month.
The flowerings are taking place at the part of the branch where farmers would normally expect to see flowers in October of this year for the 1998/99 harvest.
"It's almost as if the trees have forgotten all about the seasons," said an official at the Guaxupe cooperative in southern Minas Gerais.
"These flowers will not have time to complete their growing cycle and so they will be lost. What is worse is that they will be taking away from 1998/99 production," the official said.

Unusual weather conditions could be one of the key reasons for the flowerings, especially following a period of 17 days in September when minimum temperatures fell to below 14 degrees Celsius, not normal for the time of year, the official said.

Cooperatives in Varginha and in Franca, north of Sao Paulo state, also reported incidences of continuous flowerings. In Franca, where production is expected to reach 350,000 bags this year against last year's 550,000 bags, some 10 percent of the trees were continuing to see small flowerings.
Matiello said the phenomenon has occurred 10 years ago and is linked to weather conditions.

It happens in higher lying areas such as in southern Minas Gerais and north Sao Paulo while in Zona da Mata in Minas Gerais, it is being seen in those trees above 800 meters, said Sergio Stevanato of the cooperative in Caratinga.
But the premature flowerings should not mean any great loss to the 1998/99 crop as not all branches in one tree are affected and also the extent of the flowering depends on the variety, Matiello.
-- Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
